- **What we sell.** A **managed cold-outreach service** trading as **Milla&Vida** on the FIGSY engine. **Vida** = our operator console. **Milla** = the client portal (masked leads · 👍 approve / ✕ pass · concierge chat · meetings · reports). **Nexus** = each client's private brain. K.I.N.D remains the registered company.
- **The money, as it actually runs** (locked 24–25 Jul, #492/#541): one dollar wallet per client · first purchase **$299 = the onboarding pack, 100 approved leads included** ⛓️ *(was $99, re-locked $299 on 3 Aug, #609 — PRODUCT-RULES PR1; the 100 never moved, PR1/M1)* · then a flat **$4 per approved lead, FINAL** · no expiry, no hold, no capture-on-booking, no release · a dead email is never charged · meetings are reported, not refunded · **only the client's 👍 ever spends — operators never**. Two gates protect it: **minimum 20 approvals** the first time round, and **30 days with no approvals suspends them** (they un-suspend on their own next approval, no operator in the loop).
- **The cost floor is $352/month all-in — $146 platform + $206 company.** ⛓️ *(This bullet read **"~$457/month, not ~$190"** on 26 Jul, #556. Superseded: **`PR7`**, corrected 6 Aug, after Resend went free, Apollo went free from 3 Sep and Claude Code was downgraded ~$152 → ~$23. Floor chain: $138 "verified" → ~$146 platform (3 Aug) → **$352 all-in (6 Aug)**.)* At $4/approved the platform half alone is ~37 approvals a month, roughly one client. *(Model of record: [`CASHFLOW-LAB.html`](./CASHFLOW-LAB.html); guarded by `cost-floor-drift.test.ts`.)* And the **$99 pack was −$52 in month one** — RETIRED figure, and the reason the price moved: at **$299** (3 Aug, #609) the pack clears **≈ +$165** in month one. **The repeat is the business; the pack is the door.**

### 💼 THE TWO-MODEL DECISION — Base + Advanced, one engine *(founder-locked 31 Jul; logged 2 Aug, #608)*

**Logged late, and deliberately so.** The founder locked this on 31 Jul and then held it back: *"once we through with all this log that we need to ensure opus verifies all docs are up to date and clean. Stale docs = errors."* The cleaning is #608; this is the thing it was gating.

**The founder's case, in his words:** *"I know from my own sales experience selling a 1 product model is not strong enough… I think we need to have 2 offerings min."* He also asked not to be agreed with reflexively — *"Do not just agree with me"* — and the position below survived that challenge rather than skipping it.

**THE DECISION: Base + Advanced. Two packages, ONE engine.** Not two products, not two codebases, not two prices for the same thing. The engine that finds, scores, writes, sends, triages and books is identical in both; what differs is how much of it a client is entitled to and how much of our attention comes with it.

**Why two beats one here, on this business's own numbers:**
- **One price cannot express two buyers.** The $299 pack + $4/approved model is a single dial *(written when the pack was $99; price re-locked 3 Aug — the argument is unchanged)*. A client approving 20 leads a month and one approving 100 are the same product to us and wildly different economics — with one package the second is under-served and the first is over-sold.
- **The repeat is the business.** ⚠️ **UPDATED 3 Aug:** this said the **$99 pack is −$52 in month one**, which was true and is exactly why the price moved. At **$299** month one clears **≈ +$165** and covers acquisition too. The repeat still carries the business, but the door no longer runs at a loss. `CASHFLOW-LAB` recovers if they come back. A second tier gives a reason to come back that is not "buy more of the same".
- **Advanced is sold before it is built** — deliberately. It is a commercial position, not a build order. Nothing in Advanced should be constructed until a client has said yes to it and the price has been tested against a real conversation.

**What is NOT decided, and must not be inferred:** the price points, the exact feature split, and whether Advanced is a higher included-lead count, a higher-touch service, or an intelligence layer. Sketch figures discussed on 31 Jul ($249 Starter / $499–599 Advanced / $10–12 per lead) were **brainstorming and are not locked** — the founder said so explicitly at the time. The lock is the SHAPE: two packages, one engine.

**Coaching stays exactly as it is.** The tabbed Coaching rebuild (#601, PR #1239) is **parked on founder hold** — not cancelled, not merged. Milla's existing Coaching page is what clients see, and coaching is **not** a paid add-on: it remains a value-add on a booked meeting, which is what makes it a retention lever rather than another thing to price.

## 🏆 CREDIBILITY RULE — nothing public goes live half-full (locked 13 Jun)
> **Founder principle, applies to EVERYTHING public-facing:** we never ship a surface that looks empty or half-built — an empty Watch page, a Drop with no video, social icons linking to bare profiles, a thin Prompt Library. **Half-full = "not a real company" = lost credibility.** So: **build it fully on the branch now, but flip it LIVE only when it's genuinely populated.** Build ≠ go-live. Every website item below is gated this way (orphan/unlinked until full). Same for socials (164): icons built, hidden until the profiles have real content.

> **The principle:** Claude builds every page, all the copy, and the *video slots* **now**. The founder records video **after** and pastes it in — adding a video is a **one-line paste of a YouTube ID**, never a code change. The **Prompt Library is the one big multi-item gallery**. **Product Video / Watch page → HOLD, do not build yet.**

> ⚠️ **SUPERSEDED — 8-Jun historical snapshot, kept for the record.** Most of this was resolved 8–10 Jun: the system **deployed + is live**, **T8 + T1 passed**, a **16-test vitest suite exists**, P-a/CAL-min portal fields shipped, migration 012 ran. **The hard truths:**
1. **Nothing is deployed; nothing is end-to-end tested.** There is **no automated test suite** (no `test` script). All of D1–D5 (List-Unsubscribe, plain-text, cold-FROM), the warmup cap, P-a signer, and the admin fixes are **typecheck-clean only** — never run against a real DB, Resend, or inbox. **Typecheck ≠ working.** First real proof comes only at the Tue 9 deploy + Smoke Tests.
2. **P-a + CAL-min are backend-only → currently INERT.** No portal field exists to set `signer_name` / `booking_url`, so clients can't use them. "Done" = misleading; they're *backend-ready*, gated on UI + migration 012.
3. **Warmup cap has a blind spot.** It counts `figsy_sent_emails`, but the **day-1 batch path inserts NULL enrollment/campaign ids into NOT-NULL columns → those inserts fail → day-1 sends are never counted.** The cap reliably guards the *sequence* path only. (Pre-existing constraint bug — needs a fix or the cap to count from `outcome_events`.)
4. **`signer_name` is a latent landmine.** If the portal sends it before migration 012 runs, the `PATCH /me` upsert fails → **breaks ALL settings saves.** Migration 012 MUST run before any UI sends it.
5. **Admin still bypasses RLS.** The admin frontend uses the `service_role` key across ~13 pages — the biggest architectural security gap, **unfixed** (Week 1–2 refactor).
6. **Launch rests entirely on one un-rehearsed Tue 9 deploy** going perfectly: merge→main, run migrations 010 + 012, set/verify env vars (cold-FROM, admin key), nothing else breaks. No dry run yet.
7. **Smoke tests T1–T7 not started.** The real end-to-end verification hasn't begun. T1 (fresh signup) has never been run, ever.

**Fair risk read for Fri 19:** the *code* is in good shape and progressing fast; the **gap is verification + deploy choreography, not features.** Date is still plausible **only if** the Tue 9 deploy is clean AND Smoke Test 2 passes first try — neither is proven. Realistic buffer is thin: the day-1 cap fix, the admin RLS refactor, and any smoke-test failures all compete for the same 2–3 days. If the deploy slips or smoke tests find real breaks, **Mon 22 is the honest fallback.**

**Most valuable next moves (in order):** (1) do a **dry-run deploy to a staging/throwaway** to de-risk Tue 9; (2) **run Smoke Test T1 fresh-signup** ASAP — it's never been tested; (3) fix the day-1 cap blind spot; (4) build the P-a/CAL-min portal fields *with* migration 012 so they're actually usable.

- **19 Sep, fifth entry (THE GATE REFUSED TO SHIP A BUILD THAT WAS FINE — A TEST THAT ANSWERED DIFFERENTLY ON THE FOUNDER'S MACHINE):** ⚡ MVP1 merged to `main` (PR #1702), the founder ran `bash scripts/ship.sh`, and the gate went RED on one assertion: `xc10-frozen-tests-intact.test.ts` — *"expected '60e6e9b' to be '60e6e9ba'"*. **NOTHING WAS DEPLOYED, which was the correct outcome**, but the build being refused was sound: the failure is in the guard, not the product. 🛑 **`git rev-parse --short` IS ADAPTIVE** — git picks the shortest unambiguous abbreviation for the clone it stands in, so the certified baseline answers `60e6e9ba` in the container this build was verified in and `60e6e9b` in the founder's own clone. The test compared that machine-dependent string to a fixed 8-character literal, so it could only ever pass where git chose 8. Every gate run I made was green; his could never be. ⛓️ **AND THIS REPOSITORY HAD ALREADY PAID FOR THAT LESSON** — `ship.sh` carries it in its own words (*"`--short` picks its own abbreviation length and widens it as the repository grows"*, C-7, 17 Sep), which is why the shipped sha is `${HEAD_FULL:0:7}` and why `xc11-migration-discipline.test.ts` FORBIDS `rev-parse --short` on the shipping path. The same mistake walked back in through a test, in the one place standing in front of the release. **THE FIX:** resolve `BASELINE^{commit}` and compare the full 40-character sha as a PREFIX — length-independent, and the guard keeps its teeth because `rev-parse` still throws when the baseline is absent. **Proved across abbreviation lengths 7, 8 and 12 and the machine default (RED at 7 reproduced the founder's failure byte-identically, GREEN at all four), and proved to still FAIL on an absent baseline and on a wrong commit.** A sweep found no other executing use of `--short` that decides a test.
- **19 Sep, fourth entry (F-INBOUND — THE OPERATOR TASK IS NOW DURABLE BEFORE THE PROVIDER IS ANSWERED, AND THE RACE WAS FOUND BY A SECOND PAIR OF EYES):** ⚡ Fable's independent final verification of candidate `c00586e4` failed exactly one requirement — **F-INBOUND**: *"THE CLASSIFIER FAILED, THE REPLY WAS KEPT (1 row(s)) AND NOBODY WAS TOLD."* The builder's run of the **same SHA** had passed it. 🛑 **ONE TREE, TWO ANSWERS, AND THE PRODUCT WAS AT FAULT.** The task was raised with `void sendFounderAlert(…)` — fired into the background — so the route answered the provider **200 while the row was still in flight**, and whether a reader saw it was timing. The webhook's dedup claim is taken BEFORE processing, so a provider already told 200 **never redelivers**: a process dying in that window leaves an unclassified reply nobody is ever told about, which is precisely what R132 forbids. A wait in the harness would have hidden it. **THE FIX:** `reply-pipeline` now **awaits `raiseOperatorTask`** — the smallest primitive that writes the row — before the pipeline answers, and refuses the delivery (`unclassified_untasked` → release-and-500) if that row cannot be written, so the provider sends it again. The email mirror still goes out fire-and-forget, under the **same dedupe key**, so it cannot file a second job; `sendFounderAlert` is not what waits, because it does its Resend and Slack work first and a stranger's reply must not wait on our email vendor. The retryable-refusal list now lives beside the function that produces the codes, so Resend and Smartlead cannot diverge. **RED on the pre-fix candidate: 6 of 15 — the gate assertion proves the pipeline answered while the task was in flight; GREEN 15/15.** Keyed on the stored row, so two unclassified replies are still two jobs and a redelivery is not.

- **17 Sep, second entry (M&V FINAL MICRO-PATCH — the reply was written, the bookkeeping failed, and the exception could only be freed by hand):** ⚡ One defect, closed. R132 writes the reply BEFORE recording the outcome, deliberately — recording first would leave a resolution with no reply. But when that second write failed, the reply existed, the exception stayed **claimed**, and a retry was refused with a 409 to avoid a duplicate. Safe, and the only remaining exit was editing the database: *"Do not require the operator or Founder to manually edit the database."* ⚡ **THE ANSWER WAS ALREADY PERSISTED AND NOTHING NEW WAS BUILT.** `figsy_replies.provider_event_key` carries `unattributed:<retention id>` — written by R132 for precisely this, and protected by the pre-existing partial unique index — so one indexed read answers *was it written, and to whom*. **ZERO new migrations.** It reads **nothing else**: no sender address, no timestamp, no newest row, no candidate order, no fuzzy match, because every one of those is the guess the fail-closed design refuses and a recovery path built on one would smuggle it in where nobody looks. **Four cases:** nothing written → the R132 path byte-unchanged · exactly one → **settle only**, no reprocessing, no second classification, no second CRM push · unreadable → **fail closed** · more than one client → **fail closed, pick neither.** A retry naming a different candidate is **refused** — the persisted reply wins, and a resolution may never silently change client. Reconciliation runs **before** the claim, which is what lets it recover a claim an earlier attempt left held; it writes nothing, so `settleUnattributedReply`'s compare-and-set is guard enough and the claim code was not touched. ⚡ **AND DISCARD WAS THE SAME DEFECT'S OTHER HALF:** a reply already sitting in a client's inbox could have been recorded `discarded` — a durable lie about a client-visible record. It now refuses with a 409 naming the client and the remedy; of the two options offered, refusal beat silent auto-attribution, because Discard means *belongs to none of them* and converting that click into an attribution does something the operator did not ask for, to a client they did not name, on a surface with no undo. ➕ **THE TEETH FOUND A LEAK IN MY OWN HARNESS, and it is the lesson worth keeping:** the recovery suite reassigned its store in `beforeEach`, so a `vi.doMock` closure could keep writing into a previous test's object — the route reported success while the row under assertion stayed pristine, and the test **passed alone and failed in the full file.** Same class as the `INBOX_SECRET_KEY` process-global caught yesterday. One stable object, reset in place. **32 new assertions · 6 teeth RED then restored · 394 files / 9,093 tests · `check.sh` green · R132a chains R132.** ⚠️ **Both migrations still UNAPPLIED**; this closes none of Sprint 1, S1–S3, S4, S5/S6 runtime, House runtime or MVP1.

- **17 Sep (M&V FINAL ALIGNMENT GAP PATCH — the privacy fix had been paid for in lost mail, and now it is not):** ⚡ Two gaps closed on `claude/mvp1-full-alignment-16sep`; nothing else touched, nothing merged, nothing deployed. 🛑 **WHAT THE INDEPENDENT REVIEW FOUND, and it was right.** R131 stopped one external reply reaching two clients — and the refused reply then existed **only in process memory**. Resend's `email.received` webhook is metadata-only, so the body had been fetched into a local variable; `processed_webhook_events` stores an id and a source and nothing else; the dedup claim was already taken; and the route answered **200**, which tells the provider we have the event. It never redelivers after a 200. The only notification was `sendFounderAlert`, and **`founder_alerts` has no reader anywhere in the product** — so a correct refusal had no recovery path and the mail was simply gone. *"We must not replace a privacy leak with silent data loss."* ⚡ **PATCH 1 — DURABLE RETENTION.** `unattributed_replies` keeps the complete inbound (provider, event key, sender, recipient, subject, **fetched body**, raw payload) plus **both candidate sets as they were at ingest**, because leads move and a resolution weeks later must be checked against the clients who actually held that prospect. Nothing is reported until the row exists: on a retention failure the route **releases the dedup claim and answers 500**, the one case a webhook must not get a 200 — so while the migration is unapplied an ambiguous reply is redelivered rather than lost. ⚡ **PATCH 2 — VIDA RECOVERY, IN THE FEED THAT ALREADY EXISTS.** No new alert platform and no `founder_alerts` reader: `GET /operator/alerts` emits a `reply_unattributed` row **once per candidate client** (Vida's surface is client-scoped, so one row would be invisible to whoever was working the other client), each carrying the same `unattributed_reply_id`, and the existing chip row gains **Attribute to this client** and **Discard reply** — his wording, because with several candidates *"not ours"* is ambiguous in exactly the way the alert is. 🛑 **THE ORDER IS THE WHOLE DESIGN:** validate candidate → **claim** → write the reply → record the resolution. One column cannot do both halves — marking it resolved first loses the reply a second time when the write fails, marking it last lets two operators each write one — so the claim is a separate compare-and-set that a failed attribution hands back. The written reply goes through `processInboundReply` with one field naming the owner, which routes it down the existing `inbox` branch: **no second reply implementation, and no path back to the fan-out.** Both actions audited. ⚠️ **AND THE TEETH FOUND A REAL HOLE IN MY OWN TESTS.** Mutating `settleUnattributedReply` to drop its compare-and-set broke **nothing** — every route test was already satisfied by the handler's earlier `resolved_at` check — so the backstop that matters had never run. Three assertions were added against the store directly, and the mutation then bit. **16 teeth proved RED then restored · 78 new assertions · 9,057 tests · `check.sh` green.** ⚠️ **TWO MIGRATIONS NOW UNAPPLIED:** `20260916_client_inboxes_one_live_per_email` and `20260917_unattributed_replies`. ⚠️ **This closes none of Sprint 1, S1–S3, S4, S5/S6 runtime, House runtime or MVP1**; S5-C gained a test-only proof that a legacy credit balance cannot satisfy programme P1, with no production change.

- **15 Sep (DAY 2 · `#707` — the durability fix protected one caller and left the other):** ⚑ **INVENTORY ITEM `#707` (🟡, R121/R122)**; O1 closed at the CANONICAL boundary. 🛑 **GPT'S REVIEW WAS RIGHT AND THE DEFECT WAS MINE.** The previous round gave the handed-over sentence a stable `messageId` and moved the customer's row **above** the model call — both correct — but left `messageId` **optional**, so the ORDINARY Milla composer still sent none and the route minted a fresh uuid per request. Moving the write above the model then turned that composer's own failure path into a **duplicate factory**: send once → row A → model fails → C01 refills the composer with their sentence → they press send → **row B**. Two canonical turns for one thing said. Proven RED against `e10cd4f2`: *"one send intent produced 2 canonical customer turns"* and *"an ambiguous retry produced 2 canonical customer turns… the retry spent a second model call"*. 🛑 **SO IDENTITY NOW BELONGS TO THE SEND, NOT THE ENTRY PATH.** `millaSendIdentity` in `@kind/shared` is the ONE rule both callers pass through before the request leaves the browser: a handed-over sentence keeps the id minted at the card · **an unchanged retry of the one unresolved turn reuses its id** · anything else mints a new one. `MillaConversation` holds that intent in a ref while it is unresolved and clears it the moment the turn is answered, so **the C01 composer refill is now safe** — resubmitting is a replay the primary key absorbs, not a second turn. ⚠️ **AND IT IS NOT TEXT DEDUPLICATION.** Two deliberate *"yes"* sends are two ids and two rows because the first is resolved before the second is typed; a DIFFERENT sentence after a failure is a new turn, not a continuation. Both are asserted behaviourally. 🛑 **RELOAD RECOVERY READS THE THREAD, NOT THE BROWSER.** `unansweredCustomerTurn` finds a canonical row with no answer after it and continues it **under that row's own id** — so re-entry cannot write a second customer row and cannot re-ask a finished exchange. Canonical persistence is the truth once it owns the turn; `sessionStorage` is only the pre-ownership carrier. ⚠️ **NO SECOND SENDER, NO SECOND ENDPOINT, NO TEXT DEDUPE, NO SECOND STORE, NO MIGRATION, NO SCREEN REDESIGN.** ⚠️ **AND THE CLIENT MECHANISM IS NOW EXECUTED, NOT GREPPED** — the identity rule was extracted as pure functions precisely so the tests drive the real production code rather than a copy of it; only React's own bookkeeping around it is reproduced, and that is named in the test header. **Four teeth pulled, four bit:** the retry rule made never-reuse (E, F and the rule test fail) · made always-reuse, i.e. text dedupe (the different-sentence case and the rule test fail) · the reload continuation removed (G fails) · production stopped passing the id (the wiring guard fails). ⚠️ **AND ONE TOOTH DID NOT COMPILE ON THE FIRST ATTEMPT** — an unused-parameter error meant vitest ran against a stale `dist` and proved nothing until it was fixed; recorded, because a tooth that silently does not run is worse than one that does not bite. **Still not covered:** the React mount itself. **O2–O13 untouched. RUNTIME UNVERIFIED.** Nothing pushed, merged, deployed or migrated.

- **15 Sep (DAY 2 · `#707` — claiming the customer's sentence is not the same as owning it):** ⚑ **INVENTORY ITEM `#707` (🟡, R121/R122)**; the O1 durability correction and nothing else. 🛑 **THE HANDOFF WORKED AND STILL BROKE THE RULE.** GPT's independent review of candidate `5a1d6995` found the remaining failure inside O1: `claimMillaHandoff` **deleted** the sentence as it read it, and `POST /milla/sessions/:id/chat` called **the model first** and wrote `milla_messages` only afterwards. So a provider failure ended with **no durable customer turn anywhere** — their words lived in React state alone, and one reload made them retype. That is the founder's own rule, broken by our failure: *once the customer has sent it, we own it.* 🛑 **THE TURN IS NOW WRITTEN BEFORE THE MODEL IS ASKED**, which is the rule the Brief path has followed since 14 Sep (M6) applied to the same kind of turn one route over — and the route **fails closed** with a 503 rather than answering a question it could not record. 🛑 **AND EXACTLY-ONCE MOVED TO WHERE IT BELONGS: THE DATABASE.** Every handoff mints an `id` **once**, at stash time, which the route uses as the `milla_messages` **PRIMARY KEY** for the customer's row. A retry replays the same id, Postgres answers **23505**, and no second row exists — the repo's own existing idempotency signal (`webhook-idempotency.ts`, `morning-brief-deliver.ts`, `approve-lead.ts`), **not a new one**, and **no migration**: `milla_messages.id` has been `uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid()` since migration 008. Milla's reply row id is **derived from the customer's**, so a retry of a send that already completed **replays the stored answer and does not re-ask the model** — one sentence, one answer, whatever the network did. The claim now **leaves the sentence in `sessionStorage`** and `releaseMillaHandoff` removes it **only on a confirmed canonical turn**; `sessionStorage` survives a reload, so recovery is structural rather than hopeful. A module-level claimed-set stops StrictMode's double-mount firing two requests, and is deliberately **not** durable — a reload must be able to re-claim. ⚠️ **NO SECOND MILLA, NO NEW ENDPOINT, NO NEW STORE, NO MIGRATION, NO UI CHANGE.** **Five teeth pulled, five bit:** the stable id ignored (recovery and ambiguous retry both duplicate) · the user insert moved back below the model call (provider failure owns nothing; the retry spends a second model call) · the claim made destructive again (a failed send throws the sentence away, a reload cannot recover it) · release made unconditional (the sentence is let go with nothing owning it) · the production release unhooked. ⚠️ **AND ONE TOOTH DID NOT BITE ON THE FIRST ATTEMPT** — a destructive `removeItem` placed before the write-back line was cancelled by it, which proved nothing until it was moved; recorded because a tooth that does not bite is the defect this discipline exists to catch. **Still not covered:** the React mount itself — there is no jsdom/component-test infrastructure in this repo, so that one link is held by source-wiring guards and is named as such in both test headers. **O2–O13 untouched. RUNTIME UNVERIFIED — code cannot see production.** Nothing pushed, merged, deployed or migrated.

- **22 Aug, the atomicity correction (🔒 "TOGETHER" WAS A WORD IN MY COMMENT, NOT A PROPERTY OF THE CODE):** Independent review found the one technical defect left in the ruling I had just implemented. GO applied a held revision with **two ordinary client writes** — `figsy_campaigns.campaign_intent` first, then the ICP (targeting + activation + clearing the pending fields). Two writes across two tables are **not a transaction**. If the first landed and the second did not, the client was left with a **NEW BRIEF and OLD TARGETING** — FIGSY writing for an audience nobody had approved — while the revision could still look like it was waiting. ⚠️ **AND MY OWN COMMENT ASSERTED THE THING THAT WAS FALSE.** I had written *"a failure leaves the whole revision untouched and still waiting"* directly above the two writes, and reported it to the founder in those words. It was reasoning about the ORDER of the writes, which is not the same as atomicity and cannot substitute for it. The order I chose was the safer of the two; safer is not safe. **The fix is one `SECURITY DEFINER` function, `apply_pending_revision`, added to the same still-unapplied migration** — a plpgsql body IS one transaction, so the brief, the targeting, the one-active sweep, the activation and the clearing of all three pending fields land together, and **any raise inside rolls back every part**. The route's two writes are gone; there is one RPC call. **The two kinds of failure are separated on purpose:** bad arguments and an ICP that is not this client's are decided BEFORE any write, so they return a clean refusal rather than raising — which is also what keeps the function **probeable** (system-probes calls it with the all-zeros uuid, and the `NO_SUCH_ROW_UUID` guard caught me passing nulls). Everything that can fail after a write has landed raises. ⚠️ **The targeting is applied FIELD BY FIELD from a nine-column whitelist**, not spread from the jsonb — so a stray or hostile key in a stored payload can never reach a column nobody intended, and an absent key leaves the live value alone rather than nulling it. The PDL cursor is deliberately NOT cleared: `decideCursor` fingerprints the query and resets itself when the targeting actually changed. **PROVEN, NOT CLAIMED:** 3 RED first, including the defect in its own words — *"the new brief escaped into the live campaign while the targeting did not"* — plus two source-level guards: the shipped SQL performs BOTH updates in ONE function and raises rather than half-applying, and **the route no longer writes `figsy_campaigns` during GO at all**, so the half-apply cannot come back quietly. Two harnesses were corrected honestly rather than patched around: `kind-owns-go` asserted the two `icps` writes that no longer exist, and now asserts the transaction that replaced them. 158 tests green across nine suites · `check.sh` green (**3071 tests, 179 files**). ⚠️ **NOTHING HAS RUN ANYWHERE** — the migration is still additive and unapplied, PR #1438 is still open, and merge is the founder's (Rule 20).

The helper now has two modes: **SCAFFOLD** (the default — a `draft` row, existing rows returned untouched, no invariant consulted because a draft collides with nothing) and **ACTIVATE** (`{ activate: true }`, passed only by K.I.N.D's GO and by an operator creating an ICP in Vida). `figsy.ts` selects campaigns `.eq('status','active')`, so a draft's intent is stored and **invisible to generation until GO** — which is exactly the behaviour wanted. The default is the harmless one on purpose: a caller who forgets the flag can only fail to activate, never accidentally activate. ⚠️ **ONE CORRECTION WAS MINE, AND IT WAS MY TEST.** I asserted GO fires first sourcing after two proof passes. It does not, and should not: the ICP has already run, the standing rule is *no surprise re-spend*, and a paying client's real batch comes from the money path (`stripe.ts` → `startWorkForClient`). Sourcing at GO as well would spend twice for one decision. The assertion was wrong, not the code — corrected, with the other half (**an ICP that never ran DOES source at GO, exactly once**) added beside it so "no re-spend" can never quietly become "no sourcing ever". **PROVEN, NOT CLAIMED:** a new end-to-end journey suite drives the real handlers against one shared store — 7 RED first, naming both collisions verbatim (*"Milla stored intent and the campaign went live"* · *"refinement created a second ICP"*) — then 129 tests green across eight suites · `check.sh` green (**3052 tests, 179 files**). ⚠️ **NOTHING HAS RUN ANYWHERE** — the migration is still additive and unapplied, PR #1438 is still open, and merge is the founder's (Rule 20).

- **22 Aug, round 4 — the corrections that only showed up once the doors were closed (🚪 TAKING GO AWAY FROM THE CLIENT LEFT THEM WITH NOTHING TO PRESS):** Three of the five launch items were right in the engine and wrong at the edges, and every one was found by reading what the change did to the SURFACES rather than to the money. ⚠️ **THE DEAD BUTTON.** Making activation K.I.N.D-only was correct — and the live Milla page kept calling the activation route, so the client's *"Approve — start sourcing"* became a control that could only ever return 403. **Free proof, the launch acquisition motion, had no client entry at all.** It now has its own door, `POST /icps/:id/proof`: owns-the-ICP, prospect-only, one atomic pass, up to 20 real masked leads — and `is_active` stays **false**, because the client asks to SEE and K.I.N.D still decides when it RUNS. - **22 Aug, the launch-coherence build and its three review rounds (🎁 FREE REAL-LEAD PROOF GETS ITS OWN MONEY, AND THE FENCE WAS WRONG TWICE BEFORE IT WAS RIGHT):** Founder GO on five launch items in one PR (**#1438, open, NOT merged**): **K.I.N.D owns the GO** — a client revises their ICP freely, only an operator's green button in Vida activates it, and activating one campaign pauses the others (AR9 chained); **Milla's understanding reaches FIGSY** — the builder chat now learns the business, the campaign intent and what proof the client is permitted to claim, and writes it to `figsy_knowledge` instead of dying in a transcript; and **FREE REAL-LEAD PROOF becomes real money with a fence of its own** (AR17/AR18). ⚠️ **THE FENCE COULD NOT REUSE AR8 AND THAT WAS THE FIRST FINDING.** An unpaid prospect's `sourcing_allowance` is 0, so `try_spend_sourcing` could never have funded proof at all — and granting into that shared integer would have exposed the acquisition budget to the **six** other paths that spend it. GA removed from all 29 pages; `apps/landing` was already clean and is now pinned so. §9 rewritten to describe the real stack — it had been wrong in BOTH directions, denying GA while **failing to disclose Calendly (3 pages) and YouTube (1)**, which set their own cookies — and it now tells recipients our emails carry no pixel, the only way an invisible thing can ever be known. ⚠️ **The #605 freeze fired, which is the rule working**, and the manifest was refreshed only after his approval, never to make a red gate green. **A new guard covers what the freeze structurally cannot:** re-adding gtag AND refreshing the manifest in one PR is a green gate and a false privacy policy, so `website-no-trackers.test.ts` asserts the RELATIONSHIP between what the site loads and what it claims — in both directions, including that every vendor §9 names is actually present. **Runtime-proved in a real browser** rather than by grep: all 29 pages loaded in Chromium with every network request recorded — zero analytics hits, no `gtag`, no `dataLayer`. Reading the SDK rather than the flow found the fix was **dead on arrival**: Supabase's link shape is decided by WHICH CLIENT asks for the email, and the API sends from `@kind/db`, a plain `@supabase/supabase-js` client whose default is `flowType: 'implicit'` (auth-js `DEFAULT_OPTIONS`, read in `node_modules`). That returns the session in a **URL fragment**, and `/auth/callback` is a route handler that can only read `?code=`. **A fragment is never sent to a server.** She would have landed on *"confirmation failed"* — the identical failure `inviteUserByEmail` produced two hours earlier, for the identical reason; the mechanism changed and the defect did not. Nor would the browser rescue it: `detectSessionInUrl` **throws** `"Not a valid PKCE flow url"` on an implicit fragment when the client is PKCE. Fixed with `adoptSessionFromHash()`, which adopts the tokens explicitly and strips them from the address bar; an **open redirect** on `?next=` was closed in passing. A second, smaller bug was found and fixed first: `inviteCarriesSession` was computed from the **copyable** link and reported as if it described the **emailed** one. ⚠️ **And one of the five new guards passed for the wrong reason** — it asserted `toContain('adoptSessionFromHash')`, which the *import line* satisfies, then compared `indexOf`, where a missing call returns `-1` and sorts "before" everything. The red proof caught it. **Gate 6/6 · 2,412 tests · 5 guards red-proved.**

- **25 Jul (🔑 IPv6 SOLVED, now it's the password — and GitHub has removed the Supabase OAuth app entirely):** the pooler fallback worked: *"Tried 19 address(es); last error: **password authentication failed for user postgres**"*. That is a completely different failure from ENETUNREACH — **the database answered**, so the IPv4 route is fixed and this is now a credentials problem. Three things came out of it. ① **Supavisor reports the user as `postgres` even when we connect as `postgres.<ref>`** — it splits the dot into user + tenant — so that name in the error is expected and not evidence of a malformed username; the error text now says so, because it reads like the bug and isn't. ② **My own message was misleading:** it reported *"Tried 19 address(es)"* when the loop had stopped after two (it breaks on a non-routing error, correctly) — it printed the number of candidates GENERATED, not attempted. Fixed, and auth failures now get their own message that says plainly *"the network route is fine, this is a password problem"*, because conflating the two is what sent us chasing IPv6 twice. ③ **`passwordOf()` was truncating at the first `@`** — a generated password containing an unencoded `@` (invalid but very common in pasted connection strings) would come back short, and a short password reads back as *"password authentication failed"*: a parsing bug wearing a credentials bug's clothes. Now greedy to the last `@`, and re-encoded with `encodeURIComponent` when rebuilding. **The unblock:** the founder then reported **GitHub has removed Supabase from their authorised applications too**, so there is now no route into the Supabase dashboard at all — the password cannot be reset there. - **25 Jul (🔌 ENETUNREACH — the migration button was never going to work, and it wasn't the SQL):** the founder pressed Vida → Engine → Run it now and got `Failed: 20260725_client_inboxes — connect ENETUNREACH 2a05:d018:cb1:bb00:…:5432`. That address is **IPv6**. Supabase's direct database host (`db.<ref>.supabase.co`) has been **IPv6-only since Jan 2024** unless you pay for the IPv4 add-on, and **Railway containers have no IPv6 egress** — so the connection died before sending a byte. Nothing was wrong with the SQL, the password, or the endpoint: the address is simply unreachable from where we run, which means this button could never have worked and the whole "run migrations from Vida" workaround was resting on a connection that cannot exist. Supabase's own answer is the **pooler (Supavisor)**, which does publish IPv4: `postgres.<ref>@aws-0-<region>.pooler.supabase.com:5432` — port 5432 is SESSION mode, which behaves like a normal connection and runs DDL (6543 is transaction mode, wrong tool for migrations). The one thing not derivable is the **region**, and the founder can't look it up because the dashboard is behind the flagged GitHub account — so `lib/db-connection.ts` generates one candidate per Supabase region (SA/EU first) and the runner **probes for a reachable one before running any SQL** (so a migration is never half-applied across two different connections), then reports which host worked. Two safety details that matter: it **only** retries on routing errors (`ENETUNREACH`/`ENOTFOUND`/timeouts) and **stops dead on a credentials error**, because replaying a bad password against 18 regions is how an account gets locked out; and `safeHost()` means the response and the audit row carry host:port only, never the password. Vida's Engine now says *which* host it connected through plus a hint to set `DATABASE_URL` to the pooler string permanently, so the fallback stops being a fallback. +18 tests (`db-connection.test.ts`). Gates: api tsc + **298** vitest · admin build · doc-lint.

### 💸 THE COST FLOOR — REBUILT 3 AUG FROM ACTUAL BILLS. **~$223 was wrong. It is ~$146.**

The founder said ***"i cant afford 470/month… without income coming in this is impossible to maintain"***, and opening the real invoices found the model had been overstating the floor for weeks.

**The error, and it is the biggest single number in this repo:** the *Servers + database* line read **$138** and was tagged **verified**. All 32 outside files are now in **`supabase/migrations/`** with provenance headers and **byte-identical bodies**; originals kept (rule 3) with tombstone headers; READMEs in all three. **⚠️ One migration had NO FILE — it existed only as a string in the runner**, so the product could apply it to production while nothing described it. Recovered. **Nothing for you to do** — no production writes. ⚠️ Consolidating fixes *where things live*, not *what production has*: that is still #558, and the **Schema probe** answers six of it. | 🤖 |
| #561 🟡 | **The environment, documented — 100 vars, one table** | Done 30 Jul: **`docs/ENVIRONMENT.md`** — every variable the three apps read, its tier, **what breaks when it is unset**, and which Railway service holds it. **The old "69" was wrong twice:** a `process.env` grep cannot see the 12 vars reached by indirection, and my own scanner's comment-stripper was not regex-aware and undercounted by four. `startup-check.ts` covered **22 of 83** API vars — all 83 now carry a tier, plus two new ones: `platform` (Railway sets it, never nagged about) and **`parked`, where being SET is the fault** — `HOUSE_CLIENT_ID` un-parks #593. **Found doing it:** `INBOX_SECRET_KEY` was missing from the go-live SENDING check (✅ while nothing could send), `SUPABASE_ANON_KEY` was effectively required and listed nowhere, and `DEPLOYMENT_GUIDE.md` told you to set three portal variables **nothing reads**. **Your action: delete `PAYSTACK_SECRET_KEY` + `FLUTTERWAVE_*` from Railway, and set `INBOX_SECRET_KEY` before entering tomorrow's mailboxes.** | 🤝 |
| #317 🩷 | **Stripe refund / dispute events subscribed** | The refund, chargeback and dispute-won code all shipped and **none of it can ever fire** until Stripe → Webhooks is subscribed to `charge.refunded` · `charge.dispute.created` · `charge.dispute.closed`. A won dispute currently leaves the client permanently short. | 🧍 |
| #491 🩷 | **Per-cron failure alerting** | All 25 crons die silently if an env var is unset — one blanket alert covers the lot. With real clients sending, a dead cron is a client who stopped being worked and nobody knew. Pairs with #561. | 🤖 |
| #199 🩷 | **Nothing watches production** | There is a health probe at `index.ts:107` and **no monitor pointed at it** — no UptimeRobot, no BetterStack, no Sentry (error capture is a DB insert that swallows its own failure). If the API dies, the first person to find out is a client. | 🧍 |
| #329 🩷 | **Wipe the seed data before the first real client** | Founder-confirmed on the admin walk: *"when we flip over live we clean everything."* Test clients, seeded leads and demo residue must not sit in the database a paying client's numbers are computed from. | 🤝 |
| #298 🩷 | **The restore has never been tested** | Supabase takes backups. Nobody has ever restored one. A backup you have not restored is a belief, not a backup — and this is the only copy of every client's data. One drill, once. | 🤝 |
